subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: B3.1 — Gas exchange & B3.2 — Transport (Apr–May unit)

items.stem: Gas exchange surfaces are thin, moist and have a large surface area. The main reason for a large surface area is:
choices: To increase the rate of diffusion
items.note: Diffusion rate ∝ surface area × concentration gradient ÷ thickness. Large area and thin walls maximize diffusion; ventilation and circulation maintain the gradient.

items.stem: The main driving force for the evolution of specialized gas exchange surfaces and ventilation in large organisms is:
choices: Declining surface area-to-volume ratio as size increases
The need for more oxygen in water
items.note: As organisms get bigger, volume grows faster than surface area → simple diffusion across the surface can no longer meet oxygen demands → specialized surfaces + transport systems.

items.stem: During inhalation, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles:
choices: Contract — the diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out, lowering pressure inside the lungs
Cause pressure inside the lungs to increase
items.note: Volume increases → pressure decreases below atmospheric → air flows in. Exhalation at rest is passive (recoil).

items.stem: The alveoli are adapted for gas exchange because they are:
choices: One cell thick, moist and surrounded by a dense capillary network
items.note: Four adaptations: huge total surface area (many alveoli), single-cell thickness (short diffusion path), moist (gases dissolve), dense capillary network maintaining the concentration gradient.

items.stem: Type I pneumocytes of the alveoli are specialized for:
choices: Gas exchange — extremely thin flattened cells
items.note: Type I: ~95% of the alveolar surface, extremely thin for diffusion. Type II cells secrete surfactant to prevent the alveoli collapsing (HL).

items.stem: Which statement about the bronchioles and alveoli is correct?
choices: Bronchioles are supported by rings of cartilage
The trachea is lined with alveoli
Gas exchange occurs in the bronchi
items.note: Cartilage supports the larger airways (trachea/bronchi) and is absent in bronchioles; gas exchange happens only in the alveoli.

items.stem: In plants, most gas exchange occurs through the:
choices: Stomata in the epidermis of leaves
items.note: Stomata: pores opened and closed by guard cells. They also allow transpiration — the gas exchange/transpiration trade-off (open for CO₂ = lose water).

items.stem: Mammals have a double circulation, which means blood:
choices: Passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit
items.note: Pulmonary circulation (right heart → lungs → left heart) + systemic circulation (left heart → body → right heart). Advantages: oxygenated blood is pumped at full pressure to the tissues.

items.stem: The pacemaker of the heart — which sets the rhythm of contraction — is the:
items.note: SA node (in the right atrium) initiates each beat → atria contract → impulse reaches AV node → Purkinje fibres trigger ventricular contraction.

items.stem: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood away from the heart to the body?
items.note: Aorta = oxygenated → body. Pulmonary artery is the exception among arteries: it carries DEoxygenated blood to the lungs. Pulmonary vein: oxygenated → heart.

items.stem: Arteries have thick muscular and elastic walls because:
choices: They carry blood at high pressure
items.note: High-pressure blood from ventricular contraction. Elastic recoil smooths the pulse; muscles adjust flow. Veins: low pressure → valves prevent backflow.

items.stem: Capillaries are adapted for exchange of materials because they:
choices: Are one cell thick and highly branched, giving a large surface area
items.note: One-cell-thick walls → short diffusion distance; branching → huge surface area; narrow → red cells pass close to the wall.

items.stem: In plants, water is transported from the roots to the leaves through the:
items.note: Xylem: dead hollow tubes carrying water and minerals upwards. Phloem transports sucrose both up and down (translocation).

items.stem: The cohesion-tension theory explains water transport in xylem. Cohesion refers to:
choices: Water molecules sticking to the xylem walls
Water molecules sticking to each other via hydrogen bonds
Active pumping of water by root cells
items.note: Cohesion (water–water H-bonds) + adhesion (water–wall) + transpiration pull from the leaves = a continuous unbroken water column under tension.

items.stem: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves by:
items.note: Evaporation from spongy mesophyll cells, then diffusion out through open stomata. Rate increases with light, heat, wind and low humidity.

items.stem: Sucrose is transported in the phloem:
choices: From the roots to the leaves by transpiration pull
From sources (e.g. leaves) to sinks (e.g. roots, fruits) by active loading
In one direction only, always upwards
items.note: Translocation: active loading of sucrose into sieve tubes at the source (high pressure), unloading at the sink. Direction varies with the season — unlike xylem.

items.stem: Guard cells open the stomata when:
choices: They lose water and become flaccid
They take up water by osmosis and become turgid
CO₂ concentration inside the leaf is high
items.note: Light → potassium ions pumped in → osmotic water uptake → turgid guard cells bow apart → stoma opens. Closed at night and during water stress.

items.stem: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange.
markscheme: Numerous alveoli give a very large total surface area for diffusion (1)
Alveolar and capillary walls are one cell thick → short diffusion distance (1)
A dense capillary network surrounds each alveolus, maintaining a steep concentration gradient (1)
Moist surface — gases dissolve before diffusing (1)
Ventilation replaces the air, keeping the O₂/CO₂ gradients steep (1)
items.tactic: Link each adaptation to the diffusion equation: area, thickness, gradient. List adaptations as named structures, not just 'large lungs'.

items.stem: Outline the movement of water from the soil to the atmosphere through a plant, naming the structures involved.
markscheme: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis (1)
Water crosses the root cortex to the xylem (1)
Transpiration pull: evaporation at the leaf creates tension pulling the column up (1)
Cohesion between water molecules keeps the column unbroken; adhesion to the xylem walls supports it (1)
Water evaporates from spongy mesophyll and diffuses out through open stomata (1)
Xylem named as the transport tissue; driven by heat/light through stomata (1)
items.tactic: Trace the full path in order: soil → root hair → cortex → xylem → leaf mesophyll → stomata → atmosphere. Name every structure and the force at each step.
